items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The freedom of the central bank to set monetary policy without political interference"?
items.answer: central bank independence
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of central bank independence.

items.stem: "The central bank sets the interest rate on every loan in the economy." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It sets a policy (base) rate for lending to commercial banks; market rates follow it but also depend on risk, competition and term.
items.markingKey: It sets a policy (base) rate for lending to commercial banks; market rates follow it but also depend on risk, competition and term. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between fiscal policy and monetary policy.
items.answer: Monetary policy is run by the central bank using interest rates and the money supply; fiscal policy is run by the government using taxation and spending.
items.markingKey: Monetary policy is run by the central bank using interest rates and the money supply; fiscal policy is run by the government using taxation and spending. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that an inflation target means the central bank only cares about inflation. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Most targeting is flexible: central banks also consider output and employment (the Fed has a dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices).
items.markingKey: Most targeting is flexible: central banks also consider output and employment (the Fed has a dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Ingrid writes: "An inflation target means the central bank only cares about inflation." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Most targeting is flexible: central banks also consider output and employment (the Fed has a dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices).
items.markingKey: Most targeting is flexible: central banks also consider output and employment (the Fed has a dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that inflation targeting is the best framework for monetary policy.
items.answer: Flexible inflation targeting has worked well, but central banks also need tools for financial stability and deep recessions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: clear, transparent, anchors expectations; accountable central bank; record of low inflation since the 1990s. Arguments against: may neglect output, employment and financial stability; struggles with supply shocks; zero lower bound limits it in deep recessions. Supported judgement: Flexible inflation targeting has worked well, but central banks also need tools for financial stability and deep recessions.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "lender of last resort".
items.answer: The central bank's role of lending to commercial banks that face a liquidity crisis to prevent the banking system from collapsing
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the central bank's role of lending to commercial banks that face a liquidity crisis to prevent the banking system from collapsing. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.markingKey: Monetary policy is run by the central bank using interest rates and the money supply; fiscal policy is run by the government using taxation and spending. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe the US Federal Reserve's dual mandate and explain what it reveals about the goals of monetary policy.
items.answer: The Fed is required by law to pursue maximum employment and stable prices, interpreted as 2% PCE inflation. The Fed balances inflation and employment, for example keeping rates low in 2020-21 to support jobs
items.markingKey: Context (The Fed is required by law to pursue maximum employment and stable prices, interpreted as 2% PCE inflation.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The Fed balances inflation and employment, for example keeping rates low in 2020-21 to support jobs – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the goals of monetary policy.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Bank of England's independence in 1997 and explain what it reveals about central bank independence and inflation targeting.
items.answer: The UK government gave the Bank of England operational independence in 1997 to set interest rates to meet an inflation target set by the government. Removing short-term political influence helped anchor inflation expectations close to target for more than a decade
items.markingKey: Context (The UK government gave the Bank of England operational independence in 1997 to set interest rates to meet an inflation target set by the government.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Removing short-term political influence helped anchor inflation expectations close to target for more than a decade – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to central bank independence and inflation targeting.

items.stem: An increase in the minimum reserve requirement will:
options: reduce the amount banks can lend
items.answer: reduce the amount banks can lend
items.markingKey: C. More deposits must be kept as reserves.

items.stem: Explain why a cut in the policy interest rate can increase consumption.
items.answer: Borrowing for durables and housing becomes cheaper, saving is less rewarding, mortgage payments fall raising disposable income, and asset prices rise (wealth effect), so households spend more.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Borrowing for durables and housing becomes cheaper, saving is less rewarding, mortgage payments fall raising disposable income, and asset prices rise (wealth effect), so households spend more. items.stem: Explain the difference between expansionary monetary policy and contractionary monetary policy.
items.answer: Expansionary policy lowers interest rates or increases the money supply to raise AD; contractionary policy raises rates or reduces money supply to reduce AD and inflation.
items.markingKey: Expansionary policy lowers interest rates or increases the money supply to raise AD; contractionary policy raises rates or reduces money supply to reduce AD and inflation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe China's use of reserve requirement cuts and explain what it reveals about reserve requirements as a tool.
items.answer: The People's Bank of China repeatedly cut banks' reserve requirement ratios in 2022-2024 to support lending. Lower required reserves free funds for banks to lend, increasing the money supply
items.markingKey: Context (The People's Bank of China repeatedly cut banks' reserve requirement ratios in 2022-2024 to support lending.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Lower required reserves free funds for banks to lend, increasing the money supply – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to reserve requirements as a tool.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how a cut in the central bank's policy interest rate affects aggregate demand.
items.answer: AD/AS diagram: lower interest rates raise C (cheaper borrowing, lower saving incentive) and I (cheaper finance), and may depreciate the currency raising X − M; AD shifts right, real GDP and the price level rise.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: AD/AS diagram: lower interest rates raise C (cheaper borrowing, lower saving incentive) and I (cheaper finance), and may depreciate the currency raising X − M; AD shifts right, real GDP and the price level rise. items.stem: Outline one way in which the Federal Reserve's tightening in 2022-2023 shows contractionary monetary policy.
items.answer: The Fed raised the federal funds target range by 5.25 percentage points between March 2022 and July 2023, the fastest pace since the 1980s. Higher interest rates raised borrowing costs for mortgages and businesses, reducing AD to bring inflation down from 9.1% to about 3% by mid-2023
items.markingKey: Context (The Fed raised the federal funds target range by 5.25 percentage points between March 2022 and July 2023, the fastest pace since the 1980s.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Quantitative easing is an effective policy tool in a deep recession."
items.answer: QE helped prevent deeper recessions, but its effect on real activity is uncertain and its distributional side effects are significant.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: lowers long-term rates when policy rates are at zero; stabilises financial markets (e.g. 2008, 2020); raises asset prices and confidence. Arguments against: benefits asset holders, worsening wealth inequality; weak transmission if banks and households do not want to borrow; difficult to reverse; risk of future inflation; may create asset bubbles. Supported judgement: QE helped prevent deeper recessions, but its effect on real activity is uncertain and its distributional side effects are significant.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The buying and selling of government bonds by the central bank to change the money supply and influence interest rates"?
items.answer: open market operations
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of open market operations.

items.stem: Briefly explain why selling government bonds through open market operations is contractionary.
items.answer: Buyers pay with money from bank reserves, reducing the money supply and banks' ability to lend, which raises interest rates and reduces AD.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Buyers pay with money from bank reserves, reducing the money supply and banks' ability to lend, which raises interest rates and reduces AD. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that quantitative easing means the government prints money to pay for its spending. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Under QE the central bank buys existing bonds in financial markets to lower yields; it is a monetary operation, not direct financing of government spending.
items.markingKey: Under QE the central bank buys existing bonds in financial markets to lower yields; it is a monetary operation, not direct financing of government spending. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the Bank of England's QE programme as an example, explain quantitative easing.
items.answer: Between 2009 and 2021 the Bank of England bought £895 bn of assets, mainly government bonds. Large-scale bond purchases lowered long-term yields and supported AD when Bank Rate was near zero
items.markingKey: Context (Between 2009 and 2021 the Bank of England bought £895 bn of assets, mainly government bonds.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Large-scale bond purchases lowered long-term yields and supported AD when Bank Rate was near zero – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to quantitative easing.

items.stem: Explain why monetary policy operates with long time lags.
items.answer: Firms and households take time to change spending plans, many loans have fixed rates, and investment projects take time; the full impact on inflation can take 18-24 months.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Firms and households take time to change spending plans, many loans have fixed rates, and investment projects take time; the full impact on inflation can take 18-24 months. items.stem: Distinguish between the constraints on monetary policy and the strengths of monetary policy.
items.answer: Strengths: fast decisions, independence, incremental changes, no direct effect on debt. Constraints: time lags, the zero lower bound and liquidity traps, weak effect when confidence is low, and conflicts with growth and exchange-rate goals.
items.markingKey: Strengths: fast decisions, independence, incremental changes, no direct effect on debt. Constraints: time lags, the zero lower bound and liquidity traps, weak effect when confidence is low, and conflicts with growth and exchange-rate goals. items.stem: Using the ECB's policy for the whole euro area as an example, explain limits of a single monetary policy.
items.answer: In 2022 inflation varied from about 6% in France to over 20% in Estonia, but the ECB set one interest rate for all members. One policy rate cannot suit economies with very different inflation and growth
items.markingKey: Context (In 2022 inflation varied from about 6% in France to over 20% in Estonia, but the ECB set one interest rate for all members.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: One policy rate cannot suit economies with very different inflation and growth – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to limits of a single monetary policy.

items.stem: Briefly describe Japan's liquidity trap and explain what it reveals about constraints on monetary policy.
items.answer: The Bank of Japan cut rates to near zero in 1999 and introduced negative rates (−0.1%) in 2016, but inflation stayed below its 2% target for most of this period. With rates at the zero lower bound and weak confidence, further monetary easing had limited effects on AD
items.markingKey: Context (The Bank of Japan cut rates to near zero in 1999 and introduced negative rates (−0.1%) in 2016, but inflation stayed below its 2% target for most of this period.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: With rates at the zero lower bound and weak confidence, further monetary easing had limited effects on AD – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to constraints on monetary policy.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that monetary policy is more effective than fiscal policy at managing aggregate demand.
items.answer: Monetary policy is generally the main tool for demand management, but in deep recessions or at the zero lower bound fiscal policy is more effective.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: quick to change, set by independent experts; no impact on government debt; effective at controlling demand-pull inflation. Arguments against: weak in liquidity traps and deep recessions; long and variable time lags; cannot target specific sectors or regions; blunt and affects distribution. Supported judgement: Monetary policy is generally the main tool for demand management, but in deep recessions or at the zero lower bound fiscal policy is more effective.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "transmission mechanism"?
options: The channels through which changes in interest rates affect aggregate demand, output and inflation
The constraint that nominal interest rates cannot fall much below zero, limiting the use of rate cuts
A monetary policy framework in which the central bank publicly commits to keep inflation at a stated target, such as 2%, and adjusts interest rates to meet it
A policy where the central bank creates money to buy large amounts of government bonds and other financial assets, to lower long-term interest rates and raise the money supply

items.stem: The central bank of Sundara sets its policy rate at 0.5%; annual CPI inflation is 6%. Calculate the real interest rate and explain what it means for savers and borrowers.
items.answer: Real interest rate = 0.5 − 6 = −5.5%. Negative real rates erode the real value of savings and reduce the real cost of debt.

items.stem: A student claims that a nominal interest rate of 5% always rewards savers. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that central banks fully control the money supply.
items.answer: Central banks influence but do not fully control the money supply; commercial banks' lending decisions and the demand for credit are crucial.

items.stem: Explain why commercial banks are able to create money.
items.answer: Banks keep only a fraction of deposits as reserves; when they lend the rest, the loan is spent and redeposited in other banks, which lend again, so total deposits (money) increase by a multiple of the initial deposit.

items.stem: With reference to Japan's liquidity trap, explain how it illustrates constraints on monetary policy.
items.answer: The Bank of Japan cut rates to near zero in 1999 and introduced negative rates (−0.1%) in 2016, but inflation stayed below its 2% target for most of this period. With rates at the zero lower bound and weak confidence, further monetary easing had limited effects on AD
items.markingKey: Context (The Bank of Japan cut rates to near zero in 1999 and introduced negative rates (−0.1%) in 2016, but inflation stayed below its 2% target for most of this period.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: With rates at the zero lower bound and weak confidence, further monetary easing had limited effects on AD – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to constraints on monetary policy.

items.stem: "A nominal interest rate of 5% always rewards savers." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: If inflation is above 5% the real interest rate is negative, and the purchasing power of savings falls.
items.markingKey: If inflation is above 5% the real interest rate is negative, and the purchasing power of savings falls. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using China's use of reserve requirement cuts as an example, explain reserve requirements as a tool.
items.answer: The People's Bank of China repeatedly cut banks' reserve requirement ratios in 2022-2024 to support lending. Lower required reserves free funds for banks to lend, increasing the money supply
items.markingKey: Context (The People's Bank of China repeatedly cut banks' reserve requirement ratios in 2022-2024 to support lending.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Lower required reserves free funds for banks to lend, increasing the money supply – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to reserve requirements as a tool.

items.stem: A student claims that the central bank sets the interest rate on every loan in the economy. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It sets a policy (base) rate for lending to commercial banks; market rates follow it but also depend on risk, competition and term.
items.markingKey: It sets a policy (base) rate for lending to commercial banks; market rates follow it but also depend on risk, competition and term. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the ECB's negative interest rates as an example, explain the zero lower bound.
items.answer: The ECB's deposit rate was negative from June 2014 to July 2022, reaching −0.5%. Central banks pushed rates slightly below zero, but negative rates squeezed bank profits and had limited effects on lending
items.markingKey: Context (The ECB's deposit rate was negative from June 2014 to July 2022, reaching −0.5%.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Central banks pushed rates slightly below zero, but negative rates squeezed bank profits and had limited effects on lending – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the zero lower bound.

items.stem: With reference to the Bank of England's 2014 explanation of money creation, explain how it illustrates money creation by commercial banks.
items.answer: In 2014 the Bank of England published "Money creation in the modern economy", explaining that most money in the UK is created by commercial banks making loans. Lending decisions create new deposits, so the money supply depends heavily on banks' willingness to lend and on demand for loans
items.markingKey: Context (In 2014 the Bank of England published "Money creation in the modern economy", explaining that most money in the UK is created by commercial banks making loans.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Lending decisions create new deposits, so the money supply depends heavily on banks' willingness to lend and on demand for loans – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to money creation by commercial banks.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that quantitative easing is an effective policy tool in a deep recession.
items.answer: QE helped prevent deeper recessions, but its effect on real activity is uncertain and its distributional side effects are significant.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: lowers long-term rates when policy rates are at zero; stabilises financial markets (e.g. 2008, 2020); raises asset prices and confidence. Arguments against: benefits asset holders, worsening wealth inequality; weak transmission if banks and households do not want to borrow; difficult to reverse; risk of future inflation; may create asset bubbles. Supported judgement: QE helped prevent deeper recessions, but its effect on real activity is uncertain and its distributional side effects are significant.

items.stem: You are an economist at the trade ministry. A minister argues that inflation targeting is the best framework for monetary policy. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.
items.answer: Flexible inflation targeting has worked well, but central banks also need tools for financial stability and deep recessions.
items.markingKey: Supporting points: clear, transparent, anchors expectations; accountable central bank; record of low inflation since the 1990s. Counter-points: may neglect output, employment and financial stability; struggles with supply shocks; zero lower bound limits it in deep recessions. Recommendation: Flexible inflation targeting has worked well, but central banks also need tools for financial stability and deep recessions. Level 3 (6-8) recommendation supported but justification partly developed. Level 2 (3-5) limited justification. Level 1 (1-2) recommendation asserted.

items.stem:
Read the extract below.

In 2022 inflation varied from about 6% in France to over 20% in Estonia, but the ECB set one interest rate for all members.

The ECB's deposit rate was negative from June 2014 to July 2022, reaching −0.5%.

Using information from the extract and your knowledge of economics, evaluate the view that monetary policy is more effective than fiscal policy at managing aggregate demand.
items.answer: Monetary policy is generally the main tool for demand management, but in deep recessions or at the zero lower bound fiscal policy is more effective.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: quick to change, set by independent experts; no impact on government debt; effective at controlling demand-pull inflation. Arguments against: weak in liquidity traps and deep recessions; long and variable time lags; cannot target specific sectors or regions; blunt and affects distribution. Judgement: Monetary policy is generally the main tool for demand management, but in deep recessions or at the zero lower bound fiscal policy is more effective. Reward explicit use of the extract. items.stem: You are an economist at the trade ministry. A minister argues that central banks fully control the money supply. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.
items.answer: Central banks influence but do not fully control the money supply; commercial banks' lending decisions and the demand for credit are crucial.
items.markingKey: Supporting points: set reserve requirements and policy rates; can create reserves through QE; act as lender of last resort. Counter-points: most money is created by commercial bank lending; demand for loans depends on confidence; banks may hoard reserves (2009-2015); cash holdings and capital rules matter. Recommendation: Central banks influence but do not fully control the money supply; commercial banks' lending decisions and the demand for credit are crucial. Policy recommendation markbands [10]: Level 4 (9-10) a clear recommendation that is justified with economic theory, the information provided and its likely consequences for stakeholders; trade-offs and risks weighed. Level 3 (6-8) recommendation supported but justification partly developed. Level 2 (3-5) limited justification. Level 1 (1-2) recommendation asserted.

items.stem: Which of the following is an expansionary monetary policy?
options: The central bank buys government bonds from commercial banks
The central bank raises the reserve requirement
The central bank raises its policy rate
items.answer: The central bank buys government bonds from commercial banks
items.markingKey: A. Buying bonds increases bank reserves and the money supply.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The institution that manages a country's currency, money supply and interest rates, acts as banker to the government and commercial banks and as lender of last resort"?
items.answer: central bank
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of central bank.

items.stem: A liquidity trap is most associated with:
items.answer: Japan in the 1990s and 2000s
items.markingKey: Japan in the 1990s and 2000s. Rates near zero failed to revive spending.

items.stem: Explain why negative real interest rates may encourage borrowing.
items.answer: If inflation exceeds the nominal rate, the real value of the debt falls over time, so borrowers repay less in purchasing power than they borrowed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If inflation exceeds the nominal rate, the real value of the debt falls over time, so borrowers repay less in purchasing power than they borrowed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Zara writes: "Quantitative easing means the government prints money to pay for its spending." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Under QE the central bank buys existing bonds in financial markets to lower yields; it is a monetary operation, not direct financing of government spending.
items.markingKey: Under QE the central bank buys existing bonds in financial markets to lower yields; it is a monetary operation, not direct financing of government spending. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between fiscal policy and monetary policy.
items.answer: Monetary policy is run by the central bank using interest rates and the money supply; fiscal policy is run by the government using taxation and spending.
items.markingKey: Monetary policy is run by the central bank using interest rates and the money supply; fiscal policy is run by the government using taxation and spending. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why monetary policy may be ineffective in a liquidity trap.
items.answer: With interest rates close to zero they cannot be cut much further, and with very low confidence extra money is hoarded rather than spent, so AD does not rise.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: With interest rates close to zero they cannot be cut much further, and with very low confidence extra money is hoarded rather than spent, so AD does not rise. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Zara writes: "With a 10% reserve requirement banks will always create exactly ten times any new deposit." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: That is a maximum; banks may hold excess reserves, borrowers may not want loans and people may hold cash.
items.markingKey: That is a maximum; banks may hold excess reserves, borrowers may not want loans and people may hold cash. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Raising interest rates increases AD because savers earn more." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Higher rates usually reduce AD: borrowing and investment fall and the currency appreciates; the income gain to savers is usually smaller.
items.markingKey: Higher rates usually reduce AD: borrowing and investment fall and the currency appreciates; the income gain to savers is usually smaller. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe Türkiye's monetary policy in 2021-2023 and explain what it reveals about the importance of central bank credibility.
items.answer: Türkiye cut interest rates in 2021-22 despite rising inflation, which exceeded 80% in late 2022, before sharply reversing course in mid-2023. Perceived political pressure on the central bank damaged credibility, leading to currency depreciation and very high inflation
items.markingKey: Context (Türkiye cut interest rates in 2021-22 despite rising inflation, which exceeded 80% in late 2022, before sharply reversing course in mid-2023.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Perceived political pressure on the central bank damaged credibility, leading to currency depreciation and very high inflation – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the importance of central bank credibility.

items.stem: With reference to the ECB's policy for the whole euro area, explain how it illustrates limits of a single monetary policy.
items.answer: In 2022 inflation varied from about 6% in France to over 20% in Estonia, but the ECB set one interest rate for all members. One policy rate cannot suit economies with very different inflation and growth
items.markingKey: Context (In 2022 inflation varied from about 6% in France to over 20% in Estonia, but the ECB set one interest rate for all members.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: One policy rate cannot suit economies with very different inflation and growth – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to limits of a single monetary policy.

items.stem: Briefly describe negative real interest rates in 2022 and explain what it reveals about the real interest rate.
items.answer: In 2022 US inflation reached 9.1% while the policy rate was below 2.5% for most of the year, so real policy rates were deeply negative. Savers lost purchasing power, while the real value of fixed-rate debts fell
items.markingKey: Context (In 2022 US inflation reached 9.1% while the policy rate was below 2.5% for most of the year, so real policy rates were deeply negative.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Savers lost purchasing power, while the real value of fixed-rate debts fell – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the real interest rate.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how the central bank uses open market operations to change the money supply and interest rates.
items.answer: Money market diagram: vertical money supply MS and downward-sloping money demand; buying bonds increases MS from MS1 to MS2 and lowers the interest rate from i1 to i2.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Money market diagram: vertical money supply MS and downward-sloping money demand; buying bonds increases MS from MS1 to MS2 and lowers the interest rate from i1 to i2. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: With reference to the Bank of England's independence in 1997, explain how it illustrates central bank independence and inflation targeting.
items.answer: The UK government gave the Bank of England operational independence in 1997 to set interest rates to meet an inflation target set by the government. Removing short-term political influence helped anchor inflation expectations close to target for more than a decade
items.markingKey: Context (The UK government gave the Bank of England operational independence in 1997 to set interest rates to meet an inflation target set by the government.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Removing short-term political influence helped anchor inflation expectations close to target for more than a decade – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to central bank independence and inflation targeting.
